title: The Navy Pharmacist Who Left His Post to Open Shiseido in 1872
dek: Arinobu Fukuhara gave up a government post to open a private Western-style pharmacy in Ginza, meant to show that medicine could be reliable and prescriptions filled by a pharmacist.

story.event: Leaving the navy hospital to open a private Western-style pharmacy in Ginza
story.summary: In 1872 Arinobu Fukuhara, head of the pharmacy at Tokyo's navy hospital, resigned to open Shiseido in Ginza, described as Japan's first private Western-style pharmacy, aiming to supply reliable medicines and to separate dispensing from prescribing. The company says the new way of working was difficult at first; it went on to make medicines, Japan's first toothpaste (1888) and the lotion Eudermine (1897), and under his son Shinzo turned from pharmaceuticals to cosmetics from 1915.
paragraphs: In 1872 Arinobu Fukuhara, aged 23 by his company's account, gave up his post as head of the pharmacy at the navy hospital in Tokyo and opened a pharmacy of his own in Ginza. He called it Shiseido, after a line in the Chinese Book of Changes praising the earth from which all things are born. Shiseido describes it as Japan's first Western-style pharmacy, opened when herbal medicine was the norm.

He had trained for it since his teens. He went to Edo to study medicine, entered the shogunate's medical institute to learn Western pharmacy, and worked at the forerunner of the University of Tokyo's medical school before the navy appointment in 1871. Two things troubled him, according to the company's history and a 2015 profile in the Nikkan Kogyo Shimbun: inferior medicines were common on the market, and Japan had no system separating the doctor who prescribes from the pharmacist who dispenses. His shop was meant to show that both could be done differently.

It was hard going. Shiseido's own history says that gathering high-quality medicines and running a pharmacy in this new way was difficult at first, before the shop became known and trusted. Fukuhara kept adding to it. From 1878 Shiseido made and wholesaled medicines; in 1880 he passed the new pharmacist examination; in 1888 the shop sold what it calls Japan's first toothpaste, at about ten times the price of ordinary tooth powder; and in 1893 it offered a pill for beriberi, whose cause was then unknown.

Much of the shop's future lay elsewhere. In 1897 Shiseido launched Eudermine, a skin lotion based on the research of Dr Nagai Nagayoshi of Tokyo Imperial University and made, the company says, with the scientific methods it used for medicines. After a trip to Europe and the United States in 1900, Fukuhara installed a soda fountain in 1902. When his son Shinzo, who had studied pharmacy in Japan and at Columbia University, took charge in 1915, he moved the company from pharmaceuticals to cosmetics. Arinobu Fukuhara died in 1924, three years before Shiseido became a company limited by shares.

quote.text: It were good, therefore, that men in their innovations would follow the example of time itself; which indeed innovateth greatly, but quietly, by degrees scarce to be perceived.
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Fukuhara opened with a whole new system at once, and by his company's account it was hard going. Bacon would have counselled change by degrees, and in a sense that is what followed: trust came slowly, and the pharmacy became a cosmetics house over forty years. Which mattered more, the leap or the drift, the story leaves open.

reflection: Fukuhara was a health professional before he was a shopkeeper, and he began from a principle: reliable medicine, and a clear line between the one who prescribes and the one who dispenses. You will recognise that instinct; your own training rests on lines like it.

What grew from his principle was not what he set out to build. Toothpaste, a skin lotion and a soda fountain kept the shop known and alive, and his son turned it into something else. If your work drifts from its first shape, that need not mean the principle was wrong. It may only mean that change arrives, as Bacon says, by degrees.
invitation: Write down, in one line, the principle your work started from. Then note one way the work has changed shape since, and leave the question of whether that is good for another day.

sources.supports: Born 1848 in Awa Province; went to Edo in 1864 to study medicine; entered the shogunate's medical institute in 1865; Tokyo hospital and Daigaku Tōkō from 1869; head of the navy hospital pharmacy in 1871; resigned in 1872 and founded the Shiseido pharmacy, beginning private dispensing on the principle of separating prescribing from dispensing; passed the new pharmacist examination in 1880; 1888 toothpaste and 1897 Eudermine (Heibonsha); died 1924.

sources.title: History of Shiseido in Five Minutes
sources.supports: Fukuhara opened Japan's first private Western-style pharmacy in Ginza in 1872, applying his study of Western pharmacology and creating Japan's first separation of medical practice from dispensing; in 1916 the cosmetics department was spun off; Shiseido Co., Ltd. launched in 1927.

sources.title: World's oldest cosmetics brand: Shiseido
sources.supports: Fukuhara, educated in Western medicine and a former chief pharmacist to the navy, was dissatisfied with the quality of Japanese medicine; Japan's first toothpaste in 1888; Eudermine in 1897.

research_notes: English-language independent sources on the 1872 founding are thin; the story rests on Shiseido's own archived 'Origins' series (2009-2011), checked against the Nikkan Kogyo Shimbun's 2015 profile and three Japanese biographical dictionaries on Kotobank. Points of difference: (1) His navy post is 'chief pharmacist in a navy hospital' (Shiseido US), 'head of the Navy Hospital pharmacy' (Kotobank), 'chief of the medical office' of the navy hospital (Nikkan Kogyo) and 'Chief Pharmacist of the Japanese Navy' (Shiseido UK, NUVO); the story says head of the pharmacy at the navy hospital. (2) Age: Shiseido and Nikkan Kogyo say 23; with a birth in spring 1848 he may have been 24 by Western reckoning if the shop opened late in 1872, so the age is attributed to the company. (3) Place: one dictionary says Kyobashi, another Ginza; Ginza lay in Kyobashi ward, and the story says Ginza. (4) Heibonsha's encyclopedia says Fukuhara 'and others' formed a company, Sanseisha, that opened the pharmacy; no other source mentions partners, so the story names none, and funding is given as unknown because no source says how the shop was financed. (5) Shinzo's succession is dated 1913 by English Wikipedia (not cited) and 1915 by Shiseido's archived history; the story follows Shiseido. (6) 'Japan's first' Western-style pharmacy is the company's claim, and a search summary of an article in the journal Shashi (which could not be loaded, so is not cited) suggested a foreign-run dispensary in Yokohama opened earlier; the story therefore attributes the claim to Shiseido. The 1880 pharmacist examination comes from the Nichigai dictionary entry. Ages in Japanese sources may use traditional reckoning, so the story avoids ages for his studies. No outcome figures are used. The Bacon passage concerns innovation in general, including in states; it is applied by analogy.
